newsitem.title: JAPAN: Japan court says copyright for Popeye expired.
newsitem.headline: Japan court says copyright for Popeye expired.

text.p: Japan's Supreme Court has ruled that copyright for the popular cartoon character Popeye in Japan is no longer valid.
The ruling on Thursday overturned a 1992 lower court judgement that the country's complex 50-year copyright rule started each time a cartoon character appeared in a new media.
The copyright issue, including material like popular foreign songs, has long been a controversy between Japan and western trading blocs like the United States and the European Union.

King Features Syndicate Inc., a New York-based company which claims copyright of the spinach-eating sailorman, had filed a suit against a Japanese company for producing and selling neckties bearing the character without its permission.

Supreme Court judge Masao Fujii, in handing down Thursday's decision, said copyright on the Popeye character in Japan expired in May 1990, overturning the lower court's ruling which upheld King Features complaint.

But at the same time Judge Fujii said the Osaka-based manufacturer of the neckties had no right to use the character as while it did not breach copyright rules it violated use of the Popeye character as a legal trademark.
Under Japan's copyright law, material is protected for 50 years from the day it was first published.
